An observed signal can contain oscillations at different time scales,
with amplitudes and frequencies that vary during the record. Empirical
mode decomposition (EMD) uses the signal's local extrema to construct
components, rather than prescribing sinusoidal components of constant
frequency. `xemd` provides EMD, its extensions and related decomposition
methods, followed by operations for examining and reconstructing their
outputs.

This guide follows two examples: successive extraction by EMD
and joint fitting by variational mode decomposition (VMD). They illustrate
different meanings of a mode, the controls used to obtain it and the
diagnostics returned by the calculation. The
[methods guide](https://kanameishi.github.io/xemd/articles/methods.html) covers the other families, and
[validation and interpretation](https://kanameishi.github.io/xemd/articles/validation.html) explains the evidence
needed to select components.

## Modes and intrinsic mode functions

A mode is a component of a decomposition. In EMD, the target component is
an intrinsic mode function (IMF): its numbers of extrema and zero crossings
differ by at most one, and the mean of its upper and lower envelopes is
zero at each point. These conditions describe oscillation geometry; they allow
amplitude and frequency to vary and do not require a sinusoid of constant
frequency. The envelope mean is different from the average of all samples.

Sifting repeatedly subtracts the envelope mean to approach those
conditions. A numerical stopping rule specifies how that process ends;
an iteration limit or a prescribed number of subtractions is not proof
that the ideal IMF conditions hold. The returned diagnostics distinguish
those outcomes.

The residual signal is what remains after extraction. It can contain a
trend or a constant, and remains part of the additive reconstruction.
Neither exact reconstruction nor approximate IMF conditions establish
that a mode is a separate physical source. Different representations can
reconstruct the same signal, and one physical oscillation can be spread
over several extracted components.

## Data model

`decomposeEMD()` and `decomposeVMD()` receive a finite numeric vector
`signal`, in the units of the measured quantity. EMD operates on sample
positions. VMD also receives `samplingInterval` in seconds and center
frequencies in Hz. The [seismic records guide](https://kanameishi.github.io/xemd/articles/seismic.html) describes the
long-table interface for records, quantities and components.

The returned list depends on the method. For the EMD and VMD examples, the
fields have the following meanings:

| Field | EMD | VMD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `modes` | Matrix of samples by extracted modes | Matrix of samples by the prescribed modes |
| Remainder | `residue`, left after successive extractions | `fitResidual`, the input minus the sum of the fitted modes |
| `iterations` | Number of sifting subtractions for each mode | Number of joint sweeps, repeated for each mode |
| `converged` | Acceptance of each mode by its sifting rule | Result of the joint stopping test, repeated for each mode |
| `stopReason` | Reason extraction ended | Reason the joint iteration ended |
| `centers` | Absent | Final center frequencies in Hz |

## Empirical mode decomposition

EMD extracts a mode from the current residue and subtracts it before the
next extraction. Within an extraction, sifting subtracts the mean of the
upper and lower envelopes until the selected rule accepts the mode or the
iteration ends. The example signal contains three sines and a trend,
sampled at 3000 points. Its controls select the double-threshold rule,
reflected boundaries and up to 2000 sifting subtractions per mode;
`maxModes = Inf` lets the residue determine when extraction ends.

```{r emd}
library(xemd)

Time <- seq(0, 9, length.out = 3000)
Signal <- sin(pi * Time) + sin(2 * pi * Time) + sin(6 * pi * Time) +
    0.5 * Time
Sifting <- list(stopRule = "doubleThreshold", thresholds = c(0.05, 0.5),
                fraction = 0.05, maxSift = 2000, boundary = "reflection",
                maxModes = Inf)
EMD <- decomposeEMD(Signal, sifting = Sifting)
str(EMD)
```

`EMD$converged` describes the individual extractions: `TRUE` means that
the stopping rule accepted the mode; `FALSE` means that `maxSift` was
reached or that the envelopes could not be built. The fixed-sifting rule,
available through `decomposeEMD()`, instead reports `NA` because it
performs a prescribed number of subtractions.

`EMD$stopReason` describes the outer extraction process.
`"terminalResidue"` means that the remaining signal has at most one
extremum; `"modeLimit"` means that the requested extraction limit was
reached; `"insufficientExtrema"` means that the boundary rule could not
build the next envelopes. These reasons are separate from the acceptance
of each extracted mode.

The controls affect the decomposition itself. Envelope construction near
the record boundaries affects the extracted components, and additional
sifting can alter their amplitude modulation. The example's controls are
not a universal setting for another signal.

The sum of the modes and the residue reconstructs the signal up to
rounding. The following expression reports the largest absolute
reconstruction difference in the units of the input signal.

```{r reconstruction}
max(abs(rowSums(EMD$modes) + EMD$residue - Signal))
```

This difference checks the additive identity. It does not measure whether
each extracted component matches a generating oscillation of the signal.

`assessIMF()` provides numerical diagnostics of the IMF conditions for each column.
The `count` result tests whether the numbers of extrema and zero crossings
differ by at most one. The `deviation` result tests the envelope mean
relative to the envelope amplitude with the double threshold, an
approximation to the ideal zero envelope mean; it is `NA`
when the boundary rule cannot construct the envelopes. The example also
passes the residue as the final column, so its diagnosis remains distinct
from those of the extracted modes.

```{r assess}
assessIMF(cbind(EMD$modes, EMD$residue))
```

## Variational mode decomposition

VMD fits a prescribed number of modes concentrated around center
frequencies. It updates the mode spectra, their centers and a multiplier
together. The length of `initialCenters` sets the number of modes;
`fixedZeroCenter = FALSE` allows every center to change. VMD modes are not
defined by imposing the geometric IMF conditions of EMD. Their defining
property in this formulation is the bandwidth objective. An IMF diagnostic
can still be computed for them, but it tests a property additional to that
objective.

The signal contains tones of 2, 24 and 288 Hz sampled every millisecond.
`initialCenters` is in Hz and `alpha`, the bandwidth penalty, is in
$\mathrm{s}^2$. The expression for `alpha` converts the value 2000 from
the cycles-per-sample convention used by sktime and VMDecomp into the
units used by `xemd`. A positive `tau` selects the constrained problem;
`tau = 0` selects the penalized problem with a zero multiplier.

```{r vmd}
SamplingInterval <- 1 / 1000
TimeV <- seq_len(1000) * SamplingInterval
SignalV <- cos(2 * pi * 2 * TimeV) + 0.25 * cos(2 * pi * 24 * TimeV) +
    0.0625 * cos(2 * pi * 288 * TimeV)
VMD <- decomposeVMD(SignalV, samplingInterval = SamplingInterval,
                    initialCenters = (0:2) / (6 * SamplingInterval),
                    alpha = 2000 * SamplingInterval^2 / (8 * pi^2),
                    tau = 0.5, fixedZeroCenter = FALSE, tolerance = 1e-6,
                    maxIterations = 98)
VMD$centers
VMD$stopReason
```

`VMD$centers` contains the final center frequencies. A `stopReason` of
`"tolerance"` means that the relative change of the mode spectra passed
the stopping test; `"iterationLimit"` means that the last permitted sweep
was reached. In either case the returned modes come from the last sweep.
`VMD$fitResidual` contains the difference between the signal and their
sum; with `tau = 0`, the formulation permits a nonzero fit residual.

The prescribed mode count and bandwidth penalty affect how oscillations
are distributed among the modes. Passing the stopping test indicates
small changes between iterations; it does not certify a global optimum
or a physically unique decomposition. The returned center frequency
summarizes a mode's spectral concentration and is not its instantaneous
frequency at every sample.

## Instantaneous attributes and Hilbert spectrum

The Hilbert transform associates each real component with an analytic
signal. Its magnitude gives amplitude and its angle gives phase.
The time derivative of phase in radians, divided by $2\pi$, gives
instantaneous frequency in Hz when time is in seconds. Applying this
operation to a sum of oscillations produces the phase of that sum, not
the individual frequencies of its summands; decomposition therefore
precedes this part of Hilbert-Huang analysis.

`computeInstantaneousAttributes()` returns matrices of amplitude, phase
and frequency, with samples in rows and modes in columns. Amplitude has
the units of the input modes, phase is in radians and frequency is in Hz.
The EMD example uses a time step of 9 / 2999 seconds; the expression below
reports the median frequency of each mode.

```{r attributes}
Attributes <- computeInstantaneousAttributes(EMD$modes,
                                             samplingInterval = 9 / 2999)
apply(Attributes$frequency, 2, stats::median)
```

The analytic signal is computed by a discrete Fourier transform, which
implies periodic extension of the record. Phase is continuous within runs
of nonzero analytic amplitude; a zero leaves the phase undefined and
starts a new run. Frequency uses neighboring phase values and is `NA`
where the required phase values are undefined.

Small analytic amplitude can make the phase derivative sensitive to the
signal, and the periodic extension can affect the record boundaries.
The resulting frequency is a property of the analyzed component; its
physical interpretation also depends on how that component was separated.

`buildHilbertSpectrum()` places each instantaneous amplitude into the
cell containing its frequency, sample by sample. With `exponent = 2`, it
accumulates squared amplitudes. The edges in this example define the
intervals $[1,2)$, $[2,3)$, $[3,4)$ and $[4,5)$ in Hz.
Frequencies outside these intervals or equal to `NA` contribute nothing.

```{r spectrum}
Spectrum <- buildHilbertSpectrum(Attributes$frequency, Attributes$amplitude,
                                 edges = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), exponent = 2,
                                 samplingInterval = 9 / 2999)
Spectrum$marginal
```

`Spectrum$spectrum` holds samples by frequency cells, in squared signal
units for this example. `Spectrum$marginal` sums each cell over time and
multiplies by the sampling interval, giving squared signal units times
seconds. The values are cell masses; no division by frequency-cell width
is applied.

The marginal spectrum accumulates contributions over time and therefore
does not retain when an oscillation occurred. It is constructed from
instantaneous amplitude and frequency and is not a Fourier spectrum.

## Further reading

The [methods guide](https://kanameishi.github.io/xemd/articles/methods.html) describes method concepts, controls and
termination. The help pages for `decomposeEMD()`, `decomposeVMD()`,
`assessIMF()`, `computeInstantaneousAttributes()` and
`buildHilbertSpectrum()` specify their arguments, returned values and
references. `listOperations()` lists the exported functions and their
formal argument names.

The [bibliography](https://kanameishi.github.io/xemd/articles/references.html) lists the published work on the methods.
